name: Animal-assisted therapy
origin: Modern animal-assisted therapy is often traced to psychologist Boris Levinson, who in 1961 drew attention to the human-pet bond after finding a nonverbal child he was treating talking to his dog, and today the International Association of Human-Animal Interaction Organizations (IAHAIO) publishes standard definitions for the field (white paper 2014, updated 2018).
summary: Animal-assisted therapy (AAT) brings a trained animal, most often a dog or a horse, into planned, goal-directed treatment led by a health, education or human-service professional, with progress tracked as in any other therapy. It is the formal end of a wider family called animal-assisted interventions, which also includes informal comfort visits by trained teams (animal-assisted activities) and school-based work (animal-assisted education).
theoryOfChange: Companionship with a trained animal is thought to be an active ingredient: a calm, friendly animal comforts through body contact, can ease stress and anxious feelings, and can make it easier to open up, as in Levinson's first case. Working with an animal may also help people build skills and trusting relationships, and studies of horse-based work point to bonding, peer support, social connection and new skills as further benefits.
whatYouDo: A professional works with a trained animal, often alongside its handler, toward goals set in advance, such as easing anxiety, building trust or practicing social skills. You might sit with, stroke or play with a calm dog while talking through something hard, or take part in therapy, learning or horsemanship sessions with a horse. In animal-assisted activities, a trained team instead visits a hospital, care home or school for informal, comforting contact.
typicalDose: In the 35 trials pooled in a 2026 meta-analysis, sessions lasted 10 to 180 minutes and most often ran once or twice a week, though schedules ranged from every two weeks to eight or more sessions a week. Dogs were used in about 7 of 10 programs, and about 1 in 10 used robotic animals instead of live ones.
keyTechniques: Equine-assisted services (therapy, learning or horsemanship sessions)
Therapy with other animals, such as cats, birds or farm animals
Animal-assisted activity visits in hospitals, care homes and schools

evidence.summary: The largest recent analysis, a 2026 meta-analysis of 35 randomized trials with 2,391 adults (Shih and colleagues), found small to moderate reductions in depression and anxiety and a larger but less certain drop in stress, with no meaningful effect on pain or walking and substantial differences between studies. For horses, a 2024 review of 13 studies with 344 veterans found lower PTSD scores after equine-assisted services, but almost all of the studies were low quality (Provan and colleagues). Earlier reviews were more cautious: a 2014 systematic review found only 11 randomized trials, judged them relatively low in quality and too varied to pool, and the first meta-analysis (Nimer and Lundahl, 2007; 49 studies, not limited to randomized trials) found moderate effects. Benefits may hold mainly for people who like animals, and the wider claim that owning a pet improves health remains unproven (Herzog, 2011).

goodFitFor: People who like animals and feel calmer around them, such as children who find talk therapy hard, older adults in care homes, and some adults with anxiety, depression or trauma. Dog-assisted therapy is generally used as a complement to other therapies rather than on its own.
cautions: Allergies to animal fur and the spread of germs, especially to people with weak immune systems in hospital, are real risks, so animals should be healthy and screened, and no one should be pushed into contact, including people who fear animals. Animals can be stressed, injured or made ill by the work; enough rest, shorter sessions and a handler who reads the animal's stress signals protect them, and IAHAIO publishes welfare guidelines. If you need treatment, look for a licensed health or mental health professional who offers AAT, rather than a visiting program alone.
namingNote: The request said 'animal therapy'. The professional term is animal-assisted therapy (AAT): a goal-oriented, planned and structured intervention directed or delivered by a health, education or human-service professional, as IAHAIO defines it. This point centers on AAT, mostly with dogs and horses, and also covers lighter animal-assisted activities (informal visits by trained teams), but not simply owning a pet. For horses, US groups now use 'equine-assisted services' as the umbrella term and advise against 'equine therapy'.
